tip: मिलना (milna = to meet) takes से (se): पूजा से मिलिए (Pooja se miliye) is literally 'meet from Pooja'. In Hindi you normally meet a person through से (se), not directly.
You don't just hear in Hindi – hearing comes to you: सुनाई देने लगा (sunai dene laga) is literally 'hearing began to give'. Seeing works the same way: दिखाई देना (dikhai dena).
पूछना (poochhna) usually means 'ask', but with food it means offer: चाय-नाश्ता पूछते हैं (chai-nashta poochhte hain) = we offer tea and snacks, not ask about them.
जुगाड़ (jugaad) has no single English equivalent – a clever, improvised fix using whatever is at hand. The word covers the fix, the skill, and the mindset all at once.
English took 'thug' from Hindi ठग (thag) and 'loot' from लूट (loot) – both entered English in the colonial era. In this sentence they still mean robbers and robbing.
Hindi doubles a word with a v- echo to mean 'and such': चाय-वाय (chai-vai) = tea and whatnot. The echo वाय (vai) has no meaning of its own – it just loosens the noun.
बताना (bataana) here is not 'to tell' – the plain -ना form works as a gentle command for later: 'do let us know'. It is softer than the direct order बताओ (batao).
दोनों (donon = both) follows the pair instead of leading it: शरीर और मन दोनों (sharir aur man donon) – literally 'body and mind both'. Putting it first sounds off in Hindi.
No passive 'is called' here – subjectless कहते हैं (kahte hain) means 'people call it'. जयपुर को (Jaipur ko) marks the thing being named: people call Jaipur the Pink City.
English says ups and downs; Hindi flips the order: उतार-चढ़ाव (utaar-chadhaav) is literally 'descent-climb'. Paired opposites like this behave as a single noun.
तिल का ताड़ बनाना (til ka taad banaana) is literally 'turning a sesame seed into a palm tree' – Hindi's version of making a mountain out of a molehill.
दिल खोलकर (dil kholkar) is literally 'having opened the heart'. Hindi often uses this -कर (-kar = having done) form where English wants an adverb: wholeheartedly.
कहने को तो (kahne ko to) is literally 'for the saying' – it flags that what follows is only true on the surface, setting up the पर (par = but) that undercuts it.
रहा है (raha hai) = happening right now, like -ing: दुख रहा है (dukh raha hai = is hurting). Without रहा it reads as a habit, not this moment.
पौने (paune) = 'a quarter less': पौने सात (paune saat) = 6:45, quarter to seven. Hindi has one word per clock fraction – सवा (savaa = quarter past), साढ़े (saadhe = half past).
सी (si) after an adjective softens it: सुंदर सी ड्रेस (sundar si dress) = a rather pretty dress. It agrees too – सा (sa) with masculine nouns.
Adjectives not ending in -ा never change: गरम (garam = hot) stays the same with जून (June), चाय (chai = tea), पानी (pani = water). Only -ा adjectives shift.
For respect, even one person takes हैं (hain), not है. मेरे पिता हैं (my father is, respectful).
यह (yeh = this) for nearby, वह (woh = that) for far. यह मेरा भाई है = This is my brother.
मेरा (mera = my, m), मेरी (meri = my, f), मेरे (mere = my, m pl). The owned thing's gender picks the form.
तुम्हारा (tumhara = your, m). For feminine: तुम्हारी. For plural/respect: तुम्हारे.
मुझे (mujhe) = to me. With चाहिए (chahiye = want/need): मुझे पानी चाहिए = I want water. Super useful in any restaurant.
मुझे (mujhe) + X + पसंद है (pasand hai) = I like X. The thing liked stays unchanged. मुझे चाय पसंद है = I like tea.
Adjective matches the noun's gender. छोटा (chota, m) for boy/son. छोटी (choti) for girl/daughter.
क्या (kya) at the start = yes/no question. क्या आप X बोलते हैं? = Do you speak X?
Use कैसे (kaise = how) with masculine हो (ho, informal you). For respect: कैसे हैं? (kaise hain?).
कृपया (kripaya = please, formal). For favors, end with कीजिए (kijiye, polite command).
आइए (aaiye = come, polite command). For -ना verbs, drop -ना and add -इए for polite commands.
कल (kal) = yesterday OR tomorrow. Context decides. Future-leaning verb (मिलते हैं) here points forward: "tomorrow".
क्या (kya) in the middle means 'what'; at the very start it is a yes/no marker instead. Here it sits mid-sentence: तुम्हारा नाम क्या है (tumhara naam kya hai) = what is your name?
